name: Cheek implants
lead: Cheek implants, also called malar or submalar implants, are solid alloplastic (synthetic) devices placed over or beneath the cheekbone to increase midface projection or fullness. For appearance, a malar implant adds height and definition at the cheekbone, producing a higher, more angular contour, and a submalar implant fills a flat or hollow area below it for a fuller cheek. They are used to correct congenital cheekbone underdevelopment, asymmetry and age-related volume loss, and in gender-affirming facial surgery, and they are discussed in looksmaxxing communities as a way to obtain higher or more angular cheekbones.[1][2][3]

The usual materials are silicone and porous high-density polyethylene (sold as Medpor), with expanded PTFE (Gore-Tex) also used. The implant is typically inserted through an incision inside the mouth and stabilised with sutures or screws.[1][5][11] Reviews describe the result as permanent but reversible, since the implant can be removed.[1]

Published evidence consists mainly of reviews and case series rather than randomised trials. A 2022 review reported high patient satisfaction and low complication rates,[3] while a 2025 meta-analysis of 48 studies reported an overall complication rate of 10.7% for facial skeletal implants and 7.4% for malar implants specifically, with substantial heterogeneity between studies.[6] A 2018 systematic review found that malar implants had a high incidence of prominence problems.[5] A 2008 review noted that enthusiasm for cheek implants appeared to be declining in favour of soft-tissue approaches such as fat and fillers.[4]

Within looksmaxxing, cheek implants sit in the group of procedures often called hardmaxxing, alongside jaw and chin implants, rhinoplasty and osteotomies.[30] Forum discussion centres on implant shape, custom designs from CT scans, surgeon choice and travel for combined procedures.[18][20][22]

paras: The cheekbone (zygomatic, or malar, region) is one of the features that shapes the midface in both frontal and three-quarter views. Cheek augmentation is the group of procedures intended to emphasise this area; Wikipedia lists a solid implant over the cheekbone, injection of the patient's own fat, an injectable filler and, rarely, cuts to the zygomatic bone as the options, and notes that the procedure is often combined with a face lift or chin augmentation.[11]

Surgeons describe alloplastic malar augmentation as a reliable way to obtain permanent but reversible volume enhancement that corrects the changes of facial ageing, hypoplasia and congenital malar asymmetry. The amount of augmentation chosen depends on how severe the bony hypoplasia or soft-tissue volume loss is.[1]

Cheek implants are grouped by where they sit. Malar (shell) implants rest on the cheekbone and are intended to raise and sharpen the cheekbone contour; Wikipedia calls this the most common shape. Submalar implants sit lower and fill a hollow, flat or gaunt midface, producing a rounder cheek. Combined malar/submalar implants address both areas.[11][18]

Silicone is the most common material and is smooth and easier to remove. Porous high-density polyethylene and ePTFE are inert and integrate with surrounding tissue, which can anchor the implant but, in the case of polyethylene, may make later removal harder if a revision is needed.[5][11] Custom implants designed from CT scans are also produced, and are discussed heavily in online communities.[22][23]

Surgeons describe malar augmentation for patients with flat cheekbones, midface hypoplasia, congenital asymmetry, or volume loss from ageing.[1] An early series reported using perforated silicone implants to make the face appear more oval and youthful, and to treat congenital or traumatic cheek deficiencies.[13] A later review described implants as an occasional adjunct to orthognathic (jaw-moving) surgery, able to simulate the visual effect of osteotomies in people with skeletal deficiencies, while stating that implants are not a substitute for such surgery.[14]

Cheek augmentation is also a component of facial feminisation surgery, where high cheekbones and a full malar area are regarded as feminine features. The usual options in that setting are fillers, fat grafting and implants.[2][12] Fillers are customisable and reversible but need maintenance, fat grafting is abundant and biocompatible but has uncertain long-term retention, and implants are described as reliable but carry implant-related complications.[2] Wikipedia dates the modern field to 1982, when surgeon Douglas Ousterhout began developing facial feminisation procedures after a request from a colleague.[28] A 2019 study examined the safety of combining several facial procedures, including those on different tissue planes, in one setting for transgender facial feminisation patients.[26]

Hyaluronic acid fillers and autologous fat are less invasive, adjustable and reversible, but require repeat treatment or have uncertain long-term retention.[2] Wikipedia notes that all injected materials are eventually resorbed, and describes hyaluronic acid products such as Restylane and Juvederm as the less expensive option.[11] The dermal filler literature lists bruising and swelling as common effects and rare but serious vascular events, and states that fillers are regulated as medical devices in the United States.[29] Midface lifts, barbed-suture techniques and thread-based approaches are other soft-tissue options discussed in the literature.[4][27] A rarely used operation cuts and repositions the zygomatic bone itself, mostly in reconstructive work.[11]

In general terms, the usual surgical approach is an incision inside the mouth near the upper gum line, through which the implant is slid into a pocket over the bone. Surgeons describe the transoral approach with suture stabilisation as the most common technique for alloplastic midface augmentation.[1][11] An incision near the eye is possible but less often chosen because of the visible scar risk.[11] The operation is usually performed under sedation or general anaesthesia, takes about one to two hours, and recovery is commonly quoted at about ten days.[11] The mouth carries more bacteria than the skin, and Wikipedia notes this raises infection risk with the intraoral route.[11]

A 2022 review of recent literature concluded that overall patient satisfaction with alloplastic malar implants is high and complication rates are low, and that outcomes are likely comparable with other modalities in suitable hands.[3] A 1999 five-year retrospective review of a silicone midface implant, a 1995 series of silicone malar augmentation and a one-year multicentre evaluation of preformed augmentation shapes (including malar implants) are among the older clinical series.[15][16][7]

Most evidence is retrospective, with variable follow-up, from 2 weeks to 15 years in one review.[5] The 2008 review of midfacial rejuvenation observed that enthusiasm for cheek implants seemed to be decreasing in favour of soft-tissue treatments.[4]

General surgical risks listed by Wikipedia include infection, bleeding, blood clots and swelling; asymmetry can follow uneven resorption, displacement or shifting, and temporary loss of sensation is common, with longer-lasting loss possible.[11]

The 2018 systematic review of 626 polyethylene and 365 silicone cases found more infections and displacements with silicone, more prominence problems with polyethylene, and low exposure and extrusion rates for both. It noted that malar implants had a high incidence of prominence problems compared with chin and mandibular implants.[5]

The 2025 meta-analysis of 3,701 patients who received 4,139 implants reported pooled complication rates of 10.7% for all facial skeletal implants, 15.1% for paranasal implants and 7.4% for malar implants, with high heterogeneity.[6] Reviews also list infection, migration and visibility as implant-related complications.[2]

An analysis of adverse events and malpractice litigation related to facial implant surgery has also been published.[17] A separate study examined whether online resources about cosmetic facial surgery are reliable and understandable to patients.[25]

Silicone malar implants were being used in the 1960s; a 1975 report in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery described 52 cases since 1964, using a perforated soft silicone implant to treat flat malar eminences and congenital or traumatic deficiencies.[13] Augmentation malarplasty was reported in the early 1980s,[10] and silicone and porous implants became standard materials in subsequent decades.[16][5] A 1995 series described malar augmentation with silicone implants,[16] and a 1997 French study examined coral blocks for cheek augmentation in 23 patients.[9]

Facial feminisation surgery developed from the 1980s and made cheek augmentation a routine component of gender-affirming care.[28][12] By the 2010s and 2020s, reviews were comparing implants with fillers and fat grafting, and custom CT-designed implants were being discussed alongside stock shapes.[2][3][22]

Human data are limited to retrospective series, a small number of prospective evaluations and systematic reviews. A one-year prospective multicentre evaluation of preformed implants included 82 patients receiving nasal, chin and malar implants.[7] A prospective study of coral blocks in 23 patients was published in 1997.[9] The 2018 systematic review pooled nine polyethylene studies (626 patients) and five silicone studies (365 patients),[5] and the 2025 meta-analysis pooled 48 studies,[6] with malar implants reported in 15 of those studies (853 of 1,788 patients in those studies, 45.8%). No randomised trial comparing malar implants with other cheek augmentation methods has been published.[3][5][6]

On looksmax.org, cheek implants are discussed as a hardmaxxing option for people who consider their midface flat or recessed, sometimes as an alternative to a Le Fort III osteotomy.[18] Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing places surgery such as jaw surgery and rhinoplasty in the 'hardmaxxing' category, in contrast with 'softmaxxing' practices such as skincare and grooming.[30]

Threads cover choosing surgeons, comparing off-the-shelf and custom designs, and combining implants with other procedures such as jaw and chin implants, brow lifts or fat grafts.[18][20][21][23] Members share 3D previews of planned implants for feedback, ask whether results look too large or too small, and post questions such as how long to wait after double-jaw surgery before adding infraorbital and malar implants.[19][32][31] Some members travel abroad for multi-procedure packages, and one poster reported a cost of about US$15,000 for a package that included cheek implants.[20]
Researchers have used Google Trends data to study public interest in facial cosmetic procedures and how it relates to surgical volumes.[24]

Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery publishes a 52-case report on malar implants for facial appearance.[13]

A series on malar augmentation with silicone implants is published.[16]

A review describes the state of the art in facial feminisation surgery.[12]

Reviews of alloplastic malar implants and of cheek augmentation in gender-affirming surgery are published.[2][3]

lore.intro: Cheek implants are discussed on looksmax.org as one of several midface hardmaxxing options, with debate over implant type, design and surgeon choice, and with 3D design previews and before-and-after images shared for feedback.[18][19][21]

claims.claim: Most cheek implants are the 'apple cheek' submalar type, which gives a bloated look, while malar implants give a defined, angular look.
claims.believers: One forum member says submalar implants account for the large majority of cheek implant procedures and that malar-focused implants create a higher, more angular cheekbone effect.[18]
claims.experts: Surgical reviews describe malar, submalar and combined implants as distinct designs and discuss implant choice according to the deficiency being corrected; they do not report a standard share for each type.[1][11]

claims.claim: Custom-designed implants are better than off-the-shelf implants.
claims.believers: Community members advise custom implants over stock shapes, and some share 3D previews of designs from specific surgeons.[18][19][22]
claims.experts: Published reviews cover mainly standard implants; no comparative trial of custom versus stock cheek implants appears in the reviewed literature.[3][5]

claims.claim: Cheek implants can approximate the effect of a Le Fort III midface advancement.
claims.believers: A thread author says implants are being considered because a Le Fort III is out of reach, while a replier says infraorbital augmentation would also be needed to avoid hollowing.[18]
claims.experts: Reviews describe implants as augmenting soft tissue and bone contour, and a review of alloplastic augmentation describes it as an adjunct or alternative to orthognathic surgery but not a substitute for it.[14]

claims.claim: Implants are a safe and permanent option when done by a skilled surgeon.
claims.believers: Forum users share before-and-after results and surgeon recommendations.[19][21]
claims.experts: A 2022 review reported high satisfaction and low complication rates,[3] while a 2025 meta-analysis reported a 7.4% complication rate for malar implants[6] and reviews describe infection, migration and visibility as possible.[2]

claims.claim: Men should avoid submalar implants; submalar augmentation is for women.
claims.believers: A forum reply states that men should not augment the submalar area, describing it as the rounded 'apple cheek' look aimed at women.[18]
claims.experts: Reviews of gender-affirming surgery describe a full malar area and high cheekbones as feminine features,[2] and Wikipedia notes submalar implants are used for a gaunt or sunken midface.[11] The reviews do not set rules by sex for implant type.

claims.claim: Implants are reversible, so a bad result can be undone.
claims.believers: Community members weigh implants against filler by emphasising that they are a permanent structure and discuss revisions and second opinions on results.[31][18]
claims.experts: Reviews describe malar augmentation as permanent but reversible,[1] while Wikipedia notes that tissue ingrowth into porous polyethylene can make removal difficult.[11]

claims.claim: Multi-procedure packages abroad are a practical way to get implants and other work done at once.
claims.believers: One member posted that he was flying to Turkey for cheek implants plus a long list of other procedures for about US$15,000 and answered questions about the trip, including how to find surgeons.[20]
claims.experts: A 2019 study looked at safety when several facial procedures are combined in one setting in feminisation surgery,[26] and an analysis of facial implant malpractice cases has been published,[17] but no cited study compares outcomes of overseas packages.

card.summary: Solid silicone or polyethylene implants over the cheekbone for more projection; reviews report high satisfaction but a few percent to ~10% complication rates, and little trial-grade evidence.
card.aka: Malar implants, submalar implants, cheek augmentation
card.note: Implant-related infection, displacement and visible prominence are documented; results depend heavily on implant shape and placement.

quick.overview:
Cheek implants are solid synthetic shapes, usually silicone or porous polyethylene, placed through the mouth onto or under the cheekbone to make the midface more projected or fuller. They are used for flat cheekbones, asymmetry, ageing and facial feminisation, and are discussed on looksmaxxing forums as a way to get higher cheekbones.

Reviews of the surgical literature report high patient satisfaction and low complication rates, but the evidence is mostly retrospective series. Forum users debate malar versus submalar shapes and custom versus stock implants.
quick.mechanism: An implant is positioned over the malar bone (malar), below it (submalar) or both, and fixed with sutures or screws, adding volume and projection that is permanent unless the implant is removed.
quick.risks: A 2025 meta-analysis of 3,701 patients found a 7.4% complication rate for malar implants (10.7% across facial implants), with heterogeneity. Reported issues include infection, displacement, visible prominence and asymmetry. Implants are Rx surgical devices placed by a surgeon under anesthesia.

chain: Solid implant placed over or beneath the cheekbone
Added projection and contour in the midface
Higher, more defined or fuller cheek profile
angle.text: A malar implant adds projection over the cheekbone so the face shows a higher, more angular contour, while a submalar implant fills a flat or hollow area beneath it for a fuller midface. The change is structural and stays in place unless the implant is removed.
